old: Digital tracking with decision support and/or reminders probably makes little or no difference to some types of health outcomes, but we are uncertain about others, including maternal and neonatal deaths, because the evidence is very low-certainty [2].
new: Mobile phone-based clinical decision-support tools probably make little or no difference to some types of health outcomes, but we are uncertain about others, including maternal and neonatal deaths, because the evidence is very low-certainty [2].

old: Mobile tracking with decision support and/or client messaging (TCCMD) may increase exclusive breastfeeding among pregnant and postpartum women in settings where it is less common (RR 1.30, 95% CI 1.06 to 1.59; low-certainty evidence), but has little or no effect where almost all women breastfeed (low-certainty evidence) [3].
new: Targeted client communication via mobile devices (TCCMD) may increase exclusive breastfeeding among pregnant and postpartum women in settings where it is less common (RR 1.30, 95% CI 1.06 to 1.59; low-certainty evidence), but has little or no effect where almost all women breastfeed (low-certainty evidence) [3].

old: The effect of these mobile tracking and prompt or reminder tools on health service use is unknown because too few studies have looked at it [3].
new: For pregnant and postpartum women, the effect of these mobile tracking and prompt or reminder tools on health service use, compared with non-digital tools such as pamphlets, is unknown because too few studies have looked at it [3].

old: The effect of mobile-device tracking with decision support and/or client reminders on the proportion of births occurring in a health facility is uncertain, because the evidence is of very low certainty [3].
new: The effect of targeted client communication via mobile devices, compared with standard care, on the proportion of births occurring in a health facility among pregnant and postpartum women living with HIV is uncertain, because the evidence is of very low certainty [3].

old: The effect of targeted client communication delivered via mobile devices compared with non-digital targeted client communication is unknown, because no studies reporting this comparison were found [3].
new: In the group whose outcomes included maternal and infant adherence to antiretroviral therapy, the effect of targeted client communication delivered via mobile devices compared with non-digital targeted client communication is unknown, because no studies reporting this comparison were found [3].

The review also found, with low-certainty evidence, that the intervention "may increase the number of people with high cardiovascular disease risk‐taking prescribed aspirin (1 study, 2086 participants)" but "may make little or no difference to medication adherence among people with poorly controlled diabetes (1 study, 185 participants)" [2].

The review concludes that the use of mobile-based clinical decision-support tools "probably makes little or no difference to systolic blood pressure level among people with high cardiovascular disease risk or to the number of women giving birth in a hospital (moderate‐certainty evidence)" [2].

For decision-support tools alone, the review also found that the intervention "may make little or no difference to HbA1c levels among people with poorly controlled diabetes, or to the number of people with hyperlipidaemia reaching LDL‐cholesterol goals (low‐certainty evidence)" [2].
The qualitative synthesis also finds, with high confidence, that "the cost of messages could also be a problem" for clients, which may limit whether they receive reminder messages [4].

The same review found that adding reminders to one or more other interventions "probably improve slightly quality of care by 4.0% compared with the co‐intervention(s) without the reminder component (in 11 studies (13 comparisons), moderate‐certainty evidence)" [6].

The authors report that, in analyses looking for a 'ceiling effect' (studies with baseline adherence in the top quartile versus all others) and a floor effect (bottom quartile versus all others), they "found no indication that baseline adherence significantly affected the magnitude of effect in the intervention group" [7].

old: Digital tracking with client messaging may reduce low birthweight babies (RR 0.53) and, in stroke patients, may reduce deaths (RR 0.52) and stroke hospitalisations (RR 0.45), may slightly lower blood pressure, and may increase care-seeking for infant pneumonia or fever, while effects on stillbirths, neonatal and infant deaths, and HIV-positive antenatal tests are uncertain [1].
new: Tracking combined with decision support may reduce low birthweight babies (RR 0.53) and may increase care-seeking for infant pneumonia or fever, while effects on stillbirths, neonatal and infant deaths, and HIV-positive antenatal tests are uncertain; separately, tracking combined with client messaging, in stroke patients, may reduce deaths (RR 0.52) and stroke hospitalisations (RR 0.45) and may slightly lower systolic blood pressure [1].

old: Mobile digital tracking with decision support and/or reminders probably increases slightly the number of adults with hypertension or diabetes reporting a slightly or much better change in quality of care (one study, 3324 participants; RR 1.02, 95% CI 1.00 to 1.03), while effects on linkage to care are uncertain [1].
new: Mobile digital tracking combined with both decision support and targeted client communication probably increases slightly the number of adults with hypertension or diabetes reporting a slightly or much better change in quality of care (one study, 3324 participants; RR 1.02, 95% CI 1.00 to 1.03), while effects on linkage to care are uncertain [1].

old: For pregnant and postpartum women, the effect of these mobile tracking and prompt or reminder tools on health service use, compared with non-digital tools such as pamphlets, is unknown because too few studies have looked at it [3].
new: For pregnant and postpartum women, the effect of targeted client communication via mobile devices on health service use, compared with non-digital targeted client communication such as pamphlets, is unknown due to a lack of studies [3].

old: For pregnant and postpartum women living with HIV, tracking combined with client communication via mobile devices may make little or no difference to maternal and infant adherence to antiretroviral therapy compared with standard care (low-certainty evidence) [3].
new: For pregnant and postpartum women living with HIV, targeted client communication via mobile devices may make little or no difference to maternal and infant adherence to antiretroviral therapy compared with standard care (low-certainty evidence) [3].

old: Overall, the reviews cannot yet say with confidence that these tools improve care or health, and they call for more and better studies.
new: This summary of what the reviews conclude, and what further research they call for, cannot be checked because the reviews are not among the documents we hold.

old: For use of health services, the effect on skilled attendance at birth is uncertain (very low-certainty evidence), and the intervention may make little or no difference to antenatal influenza vaccination attendance (RR 1.05, 95% CI 0.71 to 1.58; low-certainty evidence, CI compatible with benefit and harm) [3].
new: Compared with digital non-targeted communication, the effect of targeted client communication via mobile devices on skilled attendance at birth is uncertain (very low-certainty evidence), and it may make little or no difference to antenatal influenza vaccination attendance (RR 1.05, 95% CI 0.71 to 1.58; low-certainty evidence, CI compatible with benefit and harm) [3].

new: Compared with standard care, targeted client communication via mobile devices (TCCMD) may increase exclusive breastfeeding among pregnant and postpartum women in settings where it is less common (RR 1.30, 95% CI 1.06 to 1.59; low-certainty evidence), but may have little or no effect where almost all women breastfeed (low-certainty evidence) [3].
